name: Acute Cholangitis

possible: Anaerobes (Bacteroides species) — particularly with prior biliary instrumentation or surgery
pathogens.why: Cholangitis pathogens reflect ascending enteric flora from the duodenum into an obstructed biliary tree, dominated by gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae, with anaerobes and enterococci becoming more relevant with prior instrumentation (ERCP, stents) or recurrent disease.

investigations.why: Frequently positive in cholangitis and identifies organism/susceptibility for de-escalation.
Cholestatic pattern (elevated bilirubin, ALP, GGT) supports the diagnosis and tracks resolution after drainage.
First-line imaging to identify biliary dilation and the level of obstruction.

investigations.test: MRCP or CT abdomen (if ultrasound inconclusive)
investigations.why: Better characterizes the cause and location of obstruction (stone, stricture, malignancy) to guide definitive drainage strategy.
Identifies the causative organism directly from the infected source for the most targeted de-escalation.

reason: Right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice (Charcot's triad)
, together with hypotension and altered sensorium (Reynold's pentad),

are consistent with acute cholangitis, a condition that can progress rapidly to septic shock from biliary obstruction. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started immediately, with urgent biliary drainage (ERCP or percutaneous) as the definitive source control measure — antibiotics alone are insufficient if obstruction is not relieved.

clinicalPearls: The classic presentation is Charcot's triad: biliary pain, jaundice, and spiking fevers with rigors; it is present in roughly 70% of patients with ascending cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
Addition of shock and confusion to Charcot's triad constitutes Reynolds's pentad, which signals high mortality and should trigger urgent biliary drainage (Harrison 22e p.2489).
Bile cultures are positive in approximately 75% of patients with acute cholangitis early in the symptomatic course, and blood cultures are frequently positive (Harrison 22e p.2735).
Most acute cholangitis is the nonsuppurative form, which often responds relatively quickly to supportive care and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2735).

Initial medical management (fluids and IV antibiotics) usually stabilizes the patient and buys a window of about 24 hours within which biliary drainage should be established, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489).
The bile duct may not yet be dilated on early ultrasound during acute biliary obstruction, so a normal-caliber duct does not exclude cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2489).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute cholangitis arises from infection within an obstructed biliary tree, most often due to choledocholithiasis (common duct stones complicate about 10-15% of cholelithiasis). At least partial obstruction to bile flow combined with bacterial colonization of bile produces inflammation; rising intrabiliary pressure in an obstructed system promotes translocation of organisms into the bloodstream, causing bacteremia and biliary sepsis. In suppurative cholangitis, pus accumulates under pressure within a completely obstructed duct, driving severe toxicity (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive jaundice from malignancy of the pancreatic head, bile ducts, or ampulla of Vater (often painless jaundice)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis with superimposed bacterial cholangitis
infectionMimics: Septic shock from another occult source (e.g., pneumonia, pyelonephritis) presenting before the biliary source is evident
nonInfectiousMimics: Biliary colic from choledocholithiasis (pain without fever or rigors)
Painless obstructive jaundice from neoplastic biliary obstruction
IgG4-associated (sclerosing) cholangitis, which causes biliary stricturing and is glucocorticoid-responsive
additionalInvestigations: Serum alkaline phosphatase (almost always elevated in biliary obstruction; rise may precede clinical jaundice)
Serum aminotransferases (two- to tenfold elevation, especially with acute obstruction)
ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy as the preferred initial procedure for both definitive diagnosis and therapeutic drainage
EUS as a less invasive alternative for detecting duct stones when the pretest probability of a persistent stone is lower
redFlags: Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) indicating suppurative cholangitis and high mortality
Mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock signaling suppurative cholangitis with pus under pressure
Failure to respond to antibiotics, which in suppurative disease is associated with multiple hepatic abscesses
Delay in establishing biliary drainage beyond the ~24 h stabilization window, risking recrudescent sepsis
harrison.prognosis: Nonsuppurative acute cholangitis generally responds well to antibiotics and supportive care. Suppurative acute cholangitis carries a far worse prognosis: response to antibiotics alone is poor and mortality approaches 100% unless prompt endoscopic or surgical relief of the obstruction with drainage of infected bile is achieved. Reynolds's pentad and undue delay in drainage both predict increased morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
pitfalls: Relying on antibiotics alone in suppurative cholangitis; biliary decompression is required because antibiotic response is poor and mortality is very high without it.
Excluding cholangitis because the bile duct appears non-dilated on early ultrasound, which can occur in acute obstruction.
Awaiting the full Charcot's triad before acting, since not all patients display all three components.
Mistaking the relentless toxicity of suppurative disease for simple sepsis without recognizing the need for urgent source control.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison distinguishes nonsuppurative acute cholangitis (the more common, milder form responsive to antibiotics) from suppurative acute cholangitis (pus under pressure in a completely obstructed duct, with severe toxicity, bacteremia, septic shock, and very high mortality without drainage). Clinically, Charcot's triad (pain, jaundice, fever/rigors) defines the typical syndrome, and progression to Reynolds's pentad (adding shock and confusion) marks the severe/suppurative end of the spectrum requiring urgent biliary decompression (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
